message: I have a sister named Sarah who lives in Boston.
notes: Textbook relationship extraction. Dogfood-validated case: the Stage E smoke test used the exact same message to verify the full pipeline.

message: My partner Alex and I have been together for three years.
notes: Romantic-partner relationship. Tests that 'partner' counts as a relationship category and Alex is recognized as a named Person.

message: My best friend Emma lives across the country now and I miss her a lot.
notes: Friend relationship with an emotional context. The 'miss her' emotional framing shouldn't push this into trigger territory — the persistent fact is the friendship itself.

message: I go running every morning to clear my head before work.
notes: Classic coping strategy: a named activity ('running') used routinely ('every morning') for mental health purposes ('clear my head'). Textbook USES fact.

message: I've been using breathing exercises to calm down when I feel panicky.
notes: Coping strategy with a stated trigger ('when I feel panicky'). The strategy itself is the extraction target; the panic trigger is secondary context.

message: I take fluoxetine and vyvanse daily.
notes: v0.8 dogfood case. A sentence naming two medications can be extracted as either (a) two separate USES facts, one per medication, or (b) one combined USES fact with identifier 'fluoxetine and vyvanse'. Both are defensible — the v0.8 dogfood produced (a), the v0.5-tuned prompt produces (b). The grader requires only that fluoxetine appears in some extracted USES-CopingStrategy fact; either representation passes. The split-vs-combined question will become load-bearing at v0.7 (procedural memory) or v0.9 (/memory forget granularity) and can be revisited with a prompt-level rule then. NOTE: category left unspecified — medications reasonably land as coping_strategy (mental-health tool) or context (general life situation).

message: My main goal right now is to finish my thesis by June.
notes: Stated goal with an explicit timeline. The phrase 'my main goal' is the extraction trigger; 'finish my thesis by June' is the goal content.

message: I've been wanting to switch careers into teaching for a while now.
notes: Long-term goal stated with 'for a while now' making it clearly persistent (not a passing interest). The object identifier tolerates 'teaching' or 'teach career' or similar.

message: I'm a PhD student studying climate modeling at Stanford.
notes: Stable life context — academic role, field, institution. These are persistent identity facts, not emotional content. NOTE: both object_type AND category deliberately unspecified. Across temperature=0 runs the LLM variously interprets this as (a) context/WORRIES_ABOUT/Concern, (b) context/MENTIONED_IN/Person, (c) context/WANTS/Goal (reading 'studying' as goal-pursuit), (d) goal/WANTS/Goal. All four describe the same factual content — the user's academic context — they just disagree on which ontological slot best fits. Rather than pick one and fight temperature variance, the grader requires only that SOME extracted fact mentions 'climate' (the most distinctive term in the statement). This loose check catches the regression if the extractor skips the case entirely, without breaking on legitimate framing variance.

message: I take care of my aging mother who lives with me.
notes: Caregiving context is a persistent life situation. This could arguably be category 'relationship' too (the mother is a named person) — the grader should accept either category, hence no expected category here.

message: I get really anxious whenever my supervisor schedules last-minute meetings.
notes: Trigger framed as a recurring pattern ('whenever'). The recurring-pattern framing is what makes this extractable vs 'my supervisor just scheduled a meeting' (situational, not persistent).

message: I can't stand turning in work that isn't perfect, it eats at me.
notes: Self-stated persistent pattern (perfectionism trigger). 'I can't stand' + 'eats at me' marks this as recurring/identity, not a one-off reaction.

message: I feel really sad today.
notes: Classic transient feeling — 'today' time-marker makes it explicitly temporary. Must skip per the extraction prompt's 'NEVER extract transient feelings unless named as recurring' rule.

message: I've been feeling kind of down lately.
notes: v0.4 dogfood case: 'lately' is a softer time marker than 'today' but still marks a transient feeling, not a stated recurring pattern. Must skip.

message: I'm so tired right now.
notes: Fatigue is a transient state. 'Right now' makes the time scope explicit. Must skip.

message: How do I deal with anxiety when it hits out of nowhere?
notes: Questions are not declarative statements. The prompt explicitly says to skip questions. Even though 'anxiety' is mentioned, the turn is asking for guidance, not disclosing a persistent fact.

message: Should I talk to my supervisor about how overwhelmed I'm feeling?
notes: Question asking for advice. Mentions supervisor + overwhelmed, but the turn is deliberative, not declarative. Must skip.

message: What does it mean when I keep having the same dream?
notes: Abstract question about interpretation. The 'I keep having' phrase is interesting — might tempt the extractor to pick 'relationship' or 'trigger' — but this is a question, not a statement. Must skip.

message: Thanks for that, it helps.
notes: Pure social acknowledgment. No extractable content. Must skip.

message: Hi, what can you do for me?
notes: v0.8 dogfood case: session-opening greeting + capability question. Not a fact about the user. Must skip. Cross-tests with the dispatcher case where this routes to 'supportive' — different layers, different concerns.

message: I'm scared I might not be ready for the presentation next week.
notes: Projected fear about a specific future event. Speculation, not a persistent pattern. The prompt explicitly says to skip speculation.

message: What if I'm not actually cut out for this job?
notes: Hypothetical self-doubt framed as a question. Both a question AND speculation — double disqualification. Must skip.

message: My supervisor sent a meeting invite for Monday morning and it's making me uneasy.
notes: v0.4 dogfood case: situational event with transient emotional reaction. Neither the event (one-off) nor the feeling (temporary) meets the persistence criterion. Must skip.

message: Work has been stressful this week.
notes: 'This week' marks transient context. The stress isn't framed as a recurring pattern — it's a specific week's state. Must skip.

message: I always assume one mistake means everyone will see I'm incompetent.
notes: Early-session emerging cognitive pattern. Even though the wording sounds recurring, this should be explored first rather than persisted immediately as long-term semantic memory.

message: My grandmother passed away last month and I'm still not okay with it.
notes: Bereavement disclosure — textbook 'loss' category. NOTE: object_type deliberately unspecified. The LLM interprets a loss as either object_type=Person (the lost relation) or object_type=Event (the act of passing) depending on framing. Both are defensible for this 'loss' category. We grade on category + identifier substring containing 'grandmother' — the LLM is free to build the identifier as 'grandmother' or 'grandmother passed away last month'.

message: Thanks, Sarah helped me with that.
notes: Small-talk boundary case: looks like a polite acknowledgment but contains a named relationship ('Sarah helped me'). 34 chars (under 40), but 'sarah' and 'helped' are not in SMALL_TALK_VOCABULARY, so the gate lets it through to the extractor.

message: Thanks Sarah
notes: Minimal name-only boundary case: isolates that a proper noun alone is enough to bypass the small-talk vocab gate. 'thanks' is in SMALL_TALK_VOCABULARY but 'sarah' is not.

message: ok yeah my therapist said that
notes: Small-talk boundary case: 30 chars (under 40), starts with 'ok yeah' (small-talk tokens) but 'therapist' is not in SMALL_TALK_VOCABULARY, so the vocabulary gate lets it through. Tests the vocab branch, not the length branch.

message: ok Sarah
notes: Minimal boundary case: one small-talk token ('ok') + one non-vocab token ('sarah'). Proves a single content token is enough to bypass the gate.

message: Thanks so much!
notes: Genuine small talk — pure gratitude with no extractable content. 15 chars (under 40) and all meaningful tokens ('thanks', 'much') are in SMALL_TALK_VOCABULARY.

message: ok got it
notes: Bare acknowledgment — no facts, no names, no disclosures. 9 chars and all meaningful tokens are in SMALL_TALK_VOCABULARY.

message: Thank you so much, that really helped!
notes: Gratitude at 38 chars — under the 40-char MAX_SMALL_TALK_LENGTH. The token 'helped' is NOT in SMALL_TALK_VOCABULARY, so the gate lets this through to the LLM extractor (safe false-negative). The extractor should correctly return 0 facts since there is no extractable personal information. Tests the full pipeline: gate pass-through + extractor correctly skipping pure gratitude.
